title: Bay Area Brothers Take on Western Yoga Culture in Genre-Bending Horror Film 'Namaslay'
excerpt: Filmmakers Rish and Kanish drew on personal experiences with cultural appropriation to craft a $2.5 million independent masala film that opens in theaters August 6.
body:
• Namaslay, the debut feature from Bay Area filmmaking brothers Rish and Kanish, opens exclusively in theaters on August 6, 2026, blending horror, comedy, and Indian masala storytelling to confront Western yoga culture's appropriation of Indian traditions.
  • The film follows Gayatri, a young Indian woman who stutters, as she moves to Los Angeles and discovers something sinister beneath the surface of an elite yoga studio.
  • Made independently through the duo's Junghal Studios for $2.5 million, the film features elaborate visual effects, Bharatanatyam choreography, and an orchestral score designed to rival studio-scale productions.

A pair of Indian American brothers from the Bay Area spent years watching Western wellness culture strip-mine their family's yoga practice. Now they have turned that frustration into a feature film. Namaslay, the debut from filmmakers Rish and Kanish, arrives in theaters August 6 as a genre-defying blend of horror, satire, family drama, and full-throttle Bollywood masala — all aimed squarely at what the directors call the “yoga-industrial complex.”

The film centers on Gayatri, a young Indian woman who carries memories of the yoga her grandmother taught her back home — a practice rooted in spirituality, philosophy, and physical discipline. When she moves to Los Angeles and receives an invitation to one of the city's elite yoga studios, the opportunity seems glamorous. But beneath the polished branding, something deeply sinister begins to surface.

Personal Stakes Behind the Camera

The roots of Namaslay are autobiographical. Rish and Kanish's mother practiced and taught yoga with equal emphasis on its philosophical, spiritual, and physical dimensions, but found herself pressured to dilute those teachings for Western audiences. Their father was once turned away from a Bay Area yoga studio for wearing basketball shorts instead of branded athleisure. Later, while recovering from a shoulder injury, Kanish turned to yoga himself and encountered online spaces that reduced the practice to aesthetic spectacle while ignoring its origins.

“We have a sharp message about the way Yoga has been cheapened in the west, by absurd price points, unrealistic physical standards, and of course, over-the-counter racism. For us, film is the best medium through which to speak.”

— Rish and Kanish, directors

Even the title is pointed commentary. “Namaslay” — a phrase commercialized in Western wellness culture as a cheeky twist on “Namaste” — becomes, in the filmmakers' hands, both satire and warning.

Masala for a Modern Audience

Rish and Kanish describe their film's tone as “masala,” the Indian cinematic tradition of weaving multiple genres into a single, emotionally maximalist experience. Comedy collides with horror. Suspense bleeds into musical sequences. Action erupts alongside family drama. At points, the film takes on the propulsion of a sports movie — with yoga functioning as the sport.

The filmmakers cite the anti-establishment fire of Salim-Javed classics like Deewaar and Sholay alongside modern horror touchstones like Get Out and The Sixth Sense. Gayatri herself is a layered protagonist — a person who stutters, allowing the film to explore how race, disability, gender, and culture intersect unpredictably.

An Independent Production With Studio Ambitions

Despite a reported budget of just $2.5 million, produced independently through the duo's Junghal Studios, Namaslay aims for blockbuster-scale production values. The film features elaborate visual effects, large-scale set pieces, an orchestral score, pyrotechnics, and intricate Steadicam work. One particularly demanding sequence combined blue-screen environments with Bharatanatyam choreography under severe time constraints.

“Big studios are too scared and too bloated to do what we've done,” the directors said. “Audiences today deserve films and filmmakers that respect the craft.”

What's Next

Namaslay opens exclusively in US theaters on August 6. For the Indian diaspora audience, the film represents a rare entry in American independent cinema: a story built from the specific frustrations of growing up between cultures, told in a genre language designed to be felt rather than explained. Early viewers have described the film as “an experience that can only be described as itself.” Whether mainstream audiences are ready for a masala horror film about yoga appropriation will become clear in a matter of days.
